newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan sounds warning on currencies, curbing dollar.
newsitem.headline: Japan sounds warning on currencies, curbing dollar.

text.p: Japan put another dampener on the dollar on Tuesday as top officials sounded a warning that they would not tolerate an excessively weak yen.

The comments, signalling possible intervention in the market, briefly tipped the dollar below 115 yen but the strengthening of the Japanese currency failed to dispel gloom on the stock market, where prices took another tumble amid jitters about the economy.
For the second day in a row, financial authorities voiced concern about recent moves in foreign exchange markets which saw the dollar hit its highest level in almost four years on Monday.
"An excessively weak or strong yen is not favourable for the Japanese economy," Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference on Tuesday.
"We want exchange rates to stabilise," he said.
Mitsuzuka's comments echoed remarks by Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa on Monday that Japan would continue to act appropriately to deal with excessive movements in foreign exchange markets.

"Starting from remarks by Ogawa, similar comments from many others this morning (on Tuesday) depressed the dollar buying spree," said Noriyuki Takano, assistant director of foreign exchange sales at Barclays Bank Plc in Tokyo.

But the slightly stronger yen, which normally helps the stock market because it boosts the dollar value of yen-based assets, could not snap the stock market out of its recent depression. The Tokyo stock market's key index fell more than 1.8 percent in mid-afternoon trade on Tuesday.
Ogawa's remarks in late Tokyo trade on Monday had prompted heavy sales of dollars for yen after the greenback posted a 46-month high of 117.00 yen earlier in the day.

Dealers said the remarks signalled that Japan could wade into the market and sell dollars, and helped spur a further liquidation of dollar long positions and sent the dollar down to as low as 114.90 yen. It later rebounded slightly to around 115.20 yen in early Tuesday afternoon trade.

Economic Planning Agency Minister Taro Aso also told reporters on Tuesday that wild fluctuations in foreign exchange rates were unwelcome, while Trade Minister Shinji Sato branded an excessively weak yen as troublesome for the economy.
"These remarks signal that they are ready to do something if participants try to push the dollar to 120 yen," Barclays' Takano added.

But currency dealers said the dollar was unlikely to fall below 114.50 yen, where Japanese investors were expected to sell yen related to their fresh investments in foreign securities with higher returns.

Chris Pavlou of Midland Bank Plc in Tokyo told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV): "For the time being I think they (Japanese officials) are succeeding in verbal intervention...so I think they may succeed at holding the dollar in a 114-116 yen range."
Worries about the economy have grown ahead of a planned rise in the sales tax and a planned end to special income tax cuts in April, hurting stocks.
The benchmark Nikkei 225 stock market average was down more than two percent in afternoon trade on Tuesday at 19,022.26, as dealers fretted about the future for the economy.
Concerns were lingering over "triple weakness" in Japanese financial markets in which the yen is sold as capital flows out of Japanese stocks and bonds.
